title: Intensive interaction
blurb: Use intensive interaction to connect with people at early stages of communication by following their lead and responding to them.
question: Maya, 34, has a profound and multiple learning disability and no speech. She rocks and makes humming sounds, and staff say 'you can't reach her'. How could a nurse use intensive interaction to build communication with her?

teach.body: Intensive interaction is a person-centred, responsive approach to communication. The practitioner simplifies and fine-tunes their own communication style, follows the person's lead and responds to their sounds, movements and expressions, so that the person can enjoy a two-way exchange. In plain English: you join in with what the person is already doing, and conversation grows from there. It was developed by Dave Hewett and Melanie Nind at Harperbury Hospital School in the 1980s.

teach.caption: These early skills come before speech. Intensive interaction teaches them through enjoyable shared time.

teach.body: It started with young adults at very early levels of development, many of them autistic and some showing severe behaviour that challenges. It is used with people with profound and multiple learning disabilities, autistic people with limited communication, and anyone with social communication difficulties, whatever their age. Family members can use it as well as professionals. It does not require the person to have any speech or to follow instructions.

steps.label: Tune in
steps.sub: Observe quietly; what is she doing?

teach.caption: The Institute also lists learning about feelings and developing empathy.

teach.h: Scenario: Maya in her supported living flat
teach.body: Maya, 34, rocks and hums. The community nurse sits beside her at a comfortable distance, relaxed and quiet, and watches. When Maya hums, the nurse hums the same note, then pauses. Maya stops, glances across and hums again. The nurse answers. Over ten minutes they take turns and Maya smiles. When Maya turns away, the nurse stops and stays nearby. She records what Maya started and enjoyed, so staff can repeat it daily.

teach.text: Intensive interaction is not 'copying' the person to get a task done, and it is not a ladder of stages to tick off: the Intensive Interaction Institute does not support recording progress as hierarchical 'levels'. The person leads, and records describe what they did and enjoyed over time.

items: Responsive, person-led approach: join in, pause, respond, follow.
Teaches the Fundamentals of Communication (eye contact, turn-taking, vocalisation and more).
For people at early stages of communication: PMLD, autistic people with limited communication.
Stop and stay available if the person disengages.
Record what the person did and enjoyed, not a stage reached.

summary: You can now explain intensive interaction and the Fundamentals of Communication it develops. You can run a person-led session, respond appropriately when the person disengages, and record progress in a way the approach supports.

A.q: A support worker asks what makes intensive interaction different from other communication approaches. Which answer is best?
options: Staff teach the person a set of signs in a planned order
Staff follow the person's lead and respond to what they do
Staff use objects to show the person what will happen next
Staff reward the person for each correct spoken word used
A.why: Intensive interaction is responsive and person-led: the practitioner tunes in, joins in and follows the person's lead to build a two-way exchange.

whyNot.0: Teaching signs in order describes a sign programme such as Makaton.
whyNot.2: Using objects to signal events describes objects of reference.
whyNot.3: Rewarding correct words is a directive behavioural method, not intensive interaction.

A.q: Which of the following is one of the Fundamentals of Communication described by the Intensive Interaction Institute?
options: Reading simple words
Following instructions
Turn-taking
Sorting by colour
A.why: The Fundamentals include personal space, attending, physical contact, eye contact, facial expression, turn-taking, vocalisation and enjoying being with others.

whyNot.0: Reading is a later literacy skill, not a Fundamental.
whyNot.1: Following instructions is not part of the list and is not the aim.
whyNot.3: Sorting by colour is a cognitive task, not a social communication Fundamental.

options: Andy Bondy and Lori Frost in Delaware
Carol Gray working with autistic children
Margaret Walker with two colleagues
Dave Hewett and Melanie Nind in the 1980s
A.why: Intensive interaction was developed by Dave Hewett and Melanie Nind at Harperbury Hospital School in the 1980s.

whyNot.2: Margaret Walker is associated with Makaton.

B.q: Ten minutes into an intensive interaction session, Arjun, 26, who has a profound learning disability, turns his back and covers his face. What should the nurse do?
options: Pause, give him space and stay available nearby
Gently turn him back so the session can continue
Increase her own sounds to regain his attention
End the session and note that he refused to engage
B.why: The person leads. Turning away is a message; the practitioner respects it, pauses and remains available in case he re-engages.

whyNot.1: Turning him back overrides his communication and his lead.
whyNot.2: Louder input when he has withdrawn is likely to overwhelm him.
whyNot.3: Framing it as refusal misreads the approach; he is regulating the interaction.

B.q: Staff want to record the effect of intensive interaction for Nell, 37. Which record best fits the approach?
options: The stage Nell has reached on a seven-level ladder
Observations of her eye contact and turn-taking over time
Whether she completed the planned activity each day
The number of words she has spoken during each week
B.why: Records describe what the person did, initiated and enjoyed over time. The Institute does not support hierarchical 'stages' for recording progress.

whyNot.0: The Institute does not support a hierarchical stage model of progress.
whyNot.2: Task completion is not the aim; connection and communication are.
whyNot.3: Spoken words may never be the outcome; the Fundamentals come first.

B.q: Which person is most likely to benefit from intensive interaction?
options: Faisal, 40, mild learning disability, reads easy read
Gina, 25, moderate learning disability, signs fluently
Callum, 28, profound learning disability, very limited communication
Harry, 30, mild learning disability, uses a PECS sentence strip
B.why: Intensive interaction suits people at early stages of communication, such as those with profound learning disabilities and very limited communication.

whyNot.0: Reading easy read shows established communication beyond the Fundamentals.
whyNot.1: Fluent signing shows established symbolic communication.
whyNot.3: Using a sentence strip shows he already initiates requests with pictures.

C.q: Maya, 34, has a profound and multiple learning disability. She rocks and hums. A new healthcare assistant plans to start intensive interaction by placing a ball in Maya's hands and saying 'ball' until she repeats it. What should the nurse advise?
options: Continue, as repetition is the core of the approach
Use a picture of a ball so she has a visual cue
Reward her with music each time she says the word
Start by joining in with her humming and rocking
C.why: Intensive interaction starts from what the person is already doing. Joining in with Maya's humming and rocking invites a shared, enjoyable exchange that she leads.

whyNot.0: Repeating a word and waiting for her to copy it is directive, not person-led.
whyNot.1: Adding a picture keeps the focus on a staff-set task.
whyNot.2: Rewarding speech is a behavioural teaching method, not intensive interaction.

C.q: Zak, 19, is autistic with a severe learning disability and often hits out when staff approach with tasks. His team considers intensive interaction. Which statement best supports this?
options: It is a reactive strategy to use when he hits out
It replaces the need for a functional assessment
It works by teaching him to comply with requests
It can help him feel safe and connected with staff
C.why: Reported outcomes include connection, trust and learning to regulate arousal and feel safe. It complements, rather than replaces, a functional assessment of his behaviour.

whyNot.0: Intensive interaction is a proactive, relationship-building approach; reactive strategies (NICE NG11 1.9) are what keep people safe during an incident.
whyNot.1: Behaviour that challenges still needs functional assessment (NICE NG11).
whyNot.2: Intensive interaction is person-led and does not aim at compliance.

C.q: A nurse runs intensive interaction with Lewis, 31, who has PMLD. He vocalises, she echoes, he pauses and vocalises again, smiling. Which Fundamental of Communication is most clearly developing?
options: Turn-taking
Personal space
Physical contact
Facial expression
C.why: Vocalise, echo, pause, vocalise again is an exchange of turns: the core of turn-taking.

whyNot.1: Nothing in the exchange concerns sharing space.
whyNot.3: He smiles, but the main pattern is the exchange of turns.

reteach.title: Conversation before words
reteach.question: Think of how a parent and baby 'chat' with coos and smiles before the baby can talk. What does that teach about communicating with someone who has no speech?

blocks.body: Long before words, people learn to look, take turns, make sounds on purpose and enjoy being together. Intensive interaction recreates that relaxed, responsive 'chat' for adults and children who are still at that stage, at any age, by joining in with what they already do.

blocks.text: If the person turns away, that is communication too: stop, give space and stay available.

explain.body: The practitioner simplifies their style, tunes in and follows the person's lead, responding to their sounds and movements.

test.q: In intensive interaction, who sets the content of the exchange?
options: The speech and language therapist
The person being supported
The nurse leading the session
The care plan written in advance
test.why: The person leads; the practitioner joins in with what they are doing.

whyNot.0: An SLT may advise, but the person leads the exchange.
whyNot.2: The nurse follows rather than directs.
whyNot.3: There is no set script; the person's actions shape it.

explain.body: Personal space, attending, physical contact, eye contact, facial expression, turn-taking, vocalisation and enjoying being with others.

test.q: Which is NOT one of the Fundamentals of Communication?
options: Eye contact
Vocalisation
Being with others
Matching pictures
test.why: Matching pictures is a symbolic skill; the Fundamentals are earlier social communication skills.

whyNot.2: Enjoying being with others is a Fundamental.

explain.body: If the person disengages, pause and stay available. Do not prompt, pull them back or end with a note of refusal.

test.q: A woman looks away during intensive interaction. What is the best response?
options: Call her name until she looks back
Move into her line of sight
Pause and remain available
Start a different planned activity
test.why: Looking away is a message; respecting it keeps the interaction safe and person-led.

whyNot.1: Moving into her view pursues her when she has withdrawn.
whyNot.3: Switching to a staff-chosen task removes her lead.

explain.body: Describe what the person did, started and enjoyed over time. The Institute does not support hierarchical stage-based recording.

test.q: Which note best records an intensive interaction session?
options: Reached level 3 of 7 on the ladder today
Refused to take part in the session again
Hummed, smiled when echoed, took 5 turns
Did not say any words during the session
test.why: A descriptive note of what the person started and enjoyed, including turn-taking, fits the approach.

whyNot.0: The Institute does not support hierarchical levels.
whyNot.1: Labelling refusal misreads the person's communication.
whyNot.3: Speech is not the measure of success.
